title: US Army Seeks 133,000 GMLRS Rockets by 2034 as Munitions Replenishment Accelerates; Seoul and Washington Slash Joint Drills by Half
subhead: The Army's new Sources Sought notice for 133,014 GMLRS rockets signals a nearly 36% capacity expansion on top of Lockheed Martin's current build rate, while the US-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were cut short and halved as Seoul pushes a self-reliance agenda.

sections.heading: US Army Requests 133,000 GMLRS Rockets by 2034
sections.body:
The US Army issued a Sources Sought notice this week seeking manufacturers for 133,014 Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS) rockets by 2034, Defense News reports. The plan calls for producing 19,002 rockets per year from 2028 to 2034, with first deliveries starting in February 2030. Contractors have until Sept. 1 to submit white papers.

The requirement covers unitary, alternative warhead and extended-range variants, which reach up to 150 kilometers. Current manufacturer Lockheed Martin announced last year it is ramping to 14,000 rockets annually, meaning the Army's new target requires a nearly 36% capacity increase on top of that. The notice comes as US stockpiles of GMLRS and other guided munitions have been depleted by deliveries to Ukraine and the protracted conflict with Iran, and after earlier munitions ramp-up efforts stumbled — including a 155mm shell component facility that failed to produce any parts.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest signal yet of the scale of the US guided-munitions replenishment problem: the Army is asking industry to nearly double its already-expanded GMLRS output, and the multi-year, 2034 horizon shows the Pentagon is now planning munitions production on a decade-long industrial-base footing rather than annual stopgap buys.

sections.heading: US and South Korea Slash Ulchi Freedom Shield Drills by Half
sections.body:
The US and South Korean militaries agreed to shorten the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, ending them Friday instead of Aug. 27 as originally planned, South Korean officials said Wednesday, per SCMP. The allies will complete the first, defensive phase this week and cancel the second phase involving counter-attack operations, and agreed to downsize some joint field training. The move follows President Donald Trump's order to 'substantially reduce' the drills, citing his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul's refusal to join the US war against Iran.

In parallel, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday called for accelerated efforts to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the US and to build nuclear-powered submarines, framing both as part of a broader self-reliance push. Analysts cited by SCMP said Trump's 'unpredictability' gives Lee greater strategic flexibility to advance that agenda.
sections.whyItMatters: The drill cutback is now a concrete, agreed outcome rather than a presidential order — the counter-attack phase is gone and the exercise is halved. Combined with Lee's OPCON and nuclear-submarine push, it shows the US-ROK alliance is being renegotiated in real time, with Seoul accelerating capabilities it can control independently.

sections.heading: Reliance and Rolls-Royce Enter India's Fighter Jet Engine Race
sections.body:
Indian industrial giant Reliance Industries and British engine maker Rolls-Royce announced their 'strategic intent' to form a partnership to develop an engine for India's fifth-generation Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) and set up a facility in India, SCMP reports. The proposal competes with a rival bid from French engine maker Safran and India's state-run Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), with the Cabinet Committee on Security evaluating the options.

Both competing plans reportedly promise technology transfer and intellectual property rights for engine development — a long-standing sticking point in India's effort to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers. The push follows the failure of India's indigenous Kaveri engine programme to meet the air-propulsion requirements for the Tejas light combat aircraft.
sections.whyItMatters: A Reliance-Rolls-Royce tie-up would inject serious private capital and manufacturing muscle into India's decades-long quest for an indigenous fighter engine, but analysts caution that money alone won't overcome the technical hurdles. The competition between a British-Indian consortium and Safran gives New Delhi rare leverage over technology transfer terms.

sections.heading: DARPA Lift Challenge Ends With Heavy-Lift Drone Breakthroughs
sections.body:
DARPA concluded its Lift Challenge last week with no participant hitting the goal of a drone lifting four times its own weight, but several came close, Defense News reports. AVIDrone, a Canadian company with US headquarters in Maryland, won first place and $1.25 million with its Katana heavy-lift drone, which lifted a payload-to-weight ratio of 3.84 to 1 — carrying 112.4 pounds across roughly five nautical miles on a 29.3-pound airframe.

MTech Operations took second ($750,000) at 3.64 to 1, and Xtreme Aerial Concepts third ($500,000) at 3.45 to 1. DARPA also gave a 'Most Promising Technology' award to Utah-based DefendTex, which posted the highest ratio in the competition at 9.63 to 1 but did not complete a scored run. Program manager Phillip 'Donna' Smith called heavy vertical flight the 'next great technological inflection point' for widespread adoption.
sections.whyItMatters: The results show heavy-lift drone technology is advancing rapidly toward the point where small unmanned systems can carry meaningful logistics payloads — a capability with direct military application for resupply in contested environments, and one DARPA is deliberately seeding through prize competition rather than traditional procurement.

sections.heading: US Military-Funded Research Propelled China's Robot Dogs, Reuters Finds
sections.body:
Chinese robotics firm Unitree Robotics based its most successful robot dogs on innovations funded by the US military, according to a Reuters investigation citing a former US defense technology official and three researchers involved in the project. Unitree's $1,600 Go2 model, launched in 2023, helped the company dominate the global quadruped market, and another Unitree robot has appeared on Chinese state television armed and accompanying PLA troops on an exercise.

Researchers said the designs drew on breakthroughs financed by the US Army's DEVCOM research lab, with the dimensions of Unitree's Go series 'to the millimeter' almost identical to MIT's Mini Cheetah. Unitree sold more than 5,500 humanoids and 18,000 quadrupeds last year and is valued at about $9 billion ahead of its stock market debut. In June, the Pentagon added Unitree to its list of Chinese military companies, a designation that limits future US military use of its technology.
sections.whyItMatters: The episode is a case study in how open, US-funded research can be commercialized and weaponized by a state-directed competitor: the Pentagon's own basic research helped build the robotics base that now supplies the PLA, underscoring the limits of US export controls and the challenge of competing with China's subsidized manufacturing.

sections.heading: US Naval Readiness Under Strain: Destroyer Breakdown and Foreign Shipyard Push
sections.body:
The USS Benfold, a US Navy destroyer with about 300 sailors aboard, suffered a major engineering casualty in the Pacific on July 24 that left it without power for four days, the Navy confirmed — with the crew going without drinking water, meals, functioning toilets and air conditioning, per SCMP. The incident, which became public Friday via USNI News, comes as Democratic lawmakers call for investigations into conditions aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent a record 250 uninterrupted days at sea with reported supply shortages.

Separately, President Trump last week signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum allowing foreign shipbuilders with US investments to build up to two vessels at their parent shipyards, aimed at addressing US Navy capacity gaps. South Korea's Hanwha, which took over Philadelphia's Philly Shipyard in 2024, is positioned to be among the first beneficiaries, SCMP reports.
sections.whyItMatters: The Benfold breakdown and Lincoln supply problems highlight the strain the Iran conflict has put on US naval readiness and crew quality of life, even as Washington turns to foreign shipyards to close a capacity gap it acknowledges has fallen behind strategic demand in the Indo-Pacific.

sections.heading: US Space Force and Japan Launch Second Space Surveillance Sensor
sections.body:
A US Space Force Space Domain Awareness payload launched successfully Aug. 10 aboard Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite 7, completing the second and final sensor in the Quasi-Zenith Satellite System-Hosted Payload program — the first national security space partnership of its kind between the US and Japan, Defense News reports. The payload, designed and built by MIT's Lincoln Laboratory, will deliver near-real-time data to the Space Surveillance Network, improving tracking of objects in geosynchronous orbit above the Indo-Pacific.

Mission Delta 2 will operate the sensor to identify and track objects in orbit. The first sensor launched in February 2025 on QZS-6. The program began with a December 2020 agreement between the Space Force and Japan's National Space Policy Secretariat.
sections.whyItMatters: Hosting US military sensors on Japanese navigation satellites is a notable deepening of US-Japan space cooperation, giving Washington persistent surveillance of the geosynchronous belt over the Indo-Pacific without launching dedicated US spacecraft — a model of burden-sharing in the contested space domain.

bottomLine: The dominant theme today is the US industrial base straining to rebuild what the Iran war and Ukraine deliveries have consumed: the Army's request for 133,000 GMLRS rockets by 2034 — a nearly 36% expansion on Lockheed's current rate — is the clearest measure yet of the guided-munitions shortfall, while the USS Benfold breakdown and Lincoln supply problems show the human and material cost of sustained operations. In parallel, the US-ROK alliance is being renegotiated in real time: the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills were cut short and halved, and Seoul is accelerating its own self-reliance push on OPCON and nuclear submarines. Beneath that, the technology race continues on multiple fronts — DARPA's heavy-lift drone results, India's fighter-engine competition, and the uncomfortable finding that US-funded research helped build China's robot-dog industry. The net picture is a US defense establishment pouring record sums into replenishment and industrial capacity even as its alliance and technology advantages are being tested and, in places, eroded.
sources: Defense News, SCMP, Reuters, DARPA, USNI News, Military Times
